title: Lease-based ownership and adaptive backpressure for durable partial outputs
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Problem: When clients disconnect mid-generation (intentional abort, network flaps, or mobile sleep), the serving runtime currently leaves partially materialized response state and KV cache reservations in memory for a long time or evicts them abruptly. This causes two classes of issues: cost leakage from reserved GPU/KV resources and poor UX for clients that try to resume or inspect partial outputs. Goal: introduce a lease-based ownership model for stream handlers plus an adaptive backpressure mechanism that minimizes resource waste while enabling safe resume semantics for a defined retention window.

Approach summary:
- Lease tokens: each in-flight generation is associated with a short-lived lease owned by the serving shard (lease TTL default 30s). The serving shard must renew the lease periodically while the client is actively connected or when the client sends an explicit checkpoint/ack.
- Client heartbeat and checkpoints: clients participating in long generations will be encouraged to send lightweight heartbeats or checkpoint acknowledgements. Checkpoints persist a compact resume token and minimal partial-output metadata to durable store (S3/clustered KV) to enable later resumption.
- Durable partial outputs: when a client disconnects without a checkpoint, the shard will attempt a final checkpoint and transition the generation into a tombstoned "detached" state referenced by a resume token. Detached states live for a configurable retention window (default 2 minutes) before garbage collection.
- Adaptive backpressure and preemption: backpressure is signaled proactively based on queue depth, lease pressure, and per-customer reserved capacity. If the system is near capacity, it returns a stream-level backpressure control frame (or HTTP 429 with Retry-After for simple REST) allowing clients to decide to wait, downgrade max tokens, or abort. For Dedicated pools, preemption policies allow short leases to be revoked for lower-priority tenants with graceful eviction hooks.

Acceptance criteria:
- No more than 5% increase in median latency for healthy short requests (<= 64 tokens) after enabling leases.
- Partial-output durability: resume token should restore output state and continue generation within the retention window in 90% of resumed attempts in staging tests.
- Resource leak reduction: active resource usage attributable to orphaned partial generations should drop by 70% over a 24-hr load test.
- Telemetry: new metrics (lease_renewals, detached_states_created, detached_resume_success, detached_gc_count, backpressure_signals) available in Console dashboards.

Trade-offs considered:
- Durability vs cost: persisting checkpoints increases storage I/O; we limit persisted metadata to a compact resume descriptor rather than full token KV caches.
- Complexity: adding lease and checkpoint protocol increases client and runtime complexity; therefore we default to conservative TTLs and keep resume optional.
- SLO bounds: short-lived leases and aggressive GC reduce cost but make resume window small; we make retention configurable per workspace (enterprise customers can lengthen).

Rollout plan (high level):
1) Feature flag in runtime to enable lease bookkeeping and basic backpressure signaling in staging.
2) Opt-in client SDKs: add checkpoint/heartbeat helpers in SDKs (node, python) and include sample integrations.
3) Run a canary on 5% of hosted traffic with metrics monitored.
4) Extend to Dedicated pools with tenant-level preemption configs.

Related docs: design doc and benchmark notes are linked in related_docs.
